topic: Sprix Sage Router: State-Aware SELF/COLLABORATE/HANDOFF Routing for A2A Agent Networks
primary_question: How does a state-aware router decide whether an in-flight A2A task should continue, recruit collaborators, or hand off?

competitors.title: Sprix SAGE Router: mid-execution routing for A2A networks (Zentor analysis)
key_points: Frames SAGE as the mid-execution case: the task is half done and someone must decide whether moving it is worth discarding finished work.

Publishes an older snapshot of provenance numbers: repo public 18 Aug 2026, 3,456 stars / 401 forks as of 5 Sep 2026, two releases (v0.1.0, v0.3.0 on 28 Aug), eight contributors, 43 commits, MIT, Python 3.10+, no runtime dependencies.

Reads the benchmark honestly: the progress-aware vs progress-masked utility error bars overlap (0.298 vs 0.291), so the real signal is wasted work (0.104 -> 0.059, about 43% less) and switch rate (80.1% -> 58.4%).
States the roadmap test clearly: until repeated checkpointed evaluation on real endpoints or marketplace trace replay lands, 'every number in the README is a simulation arguing with itself'.
Gap to exploit: analysis-first, no implementation walkthrough, and it is a hosted-product blog that pivots to a sales CTA (Zentor cloud machine).

competitors.title: A2A Connected the Agents. Now Someone Has to Route Them. (heatdrop, 22 Aug 2026)
key_points: Positions SAGE in the stack: A2A solved agent discovery, which is a directory problem; the runtime question of who does the work after the handshake was left open.
Documents the utility structure: predicted success minus cost, critical-path latency, risk, context-transfer loss and coordination overhead, with uncertainty and exploration terms.
Explains complementarity over prestige: a team is scored for marginal requirement coverage, not for stacking famous agents.

Lists the A2A-to-SAGE mapping (AgentCard.skills -> capability vectors, security requirements -> hard permission filters, provider quotes -> structured bids) and notes the prototype returns a decision but does not transmit tasks.

Carries a stale live star widget (about 4.3k with '+431 stars/day') and an early-launch figure of roughly 677 stars in the body text, and quotes pre-release benchmark numbers (0.634 quality vs 0.507 incumbent-only, deadline misses 26.4% -> 0.2%) that do not match current v0.3 tables.

competitors.title: Sprix SAGE makes agent routing a stateful scheduling problem (dev.to, 22 Aug 2026)
key_points: Reframes the novelty as scheduling rather than discovery: routing must account for work already completed, the cost of moving context, and the dependencies still blocking a task.

Credits the strongest design judgement: a router needs an explicit reason not to recruit, because every participant adds messages, dependencies, conflicting estimates and an attribution problem when the task fails.
Treats permission and compatibility filtering before scoring as more than an implementation detail, because a ranking model must never recommend an agent that cannot meet a security requirement.
Explains that coverage and team scoring moved from noisy-OR over all selected teammates to assigned-owner checkpoint-adjusted coverage.

Pushes on the unresolved attribution question the prototype cannot settle: whether outcome feedback reflects agent quality, task difficulty, or the router's own prior choices; also quotes older pre-v0.3 numbers (Online 0.634/0.487, deadline miss 0.2%).

competitors.title: Sprix SAGE Router directory review (FollowAgents, FA score 69/100 - 'Some gaps')
key_points: Independent directory review with an explicit scoring verdict: 69/100, 'Some gaps'.

Lists five concrete adoption profiles (A2A orchestrator team, MAS researcher comparing the three modes, marketplace team needing per-agent-per-requirement reliability, workflow architect designing failure recovery, routing-algorithm team needing deterministic replay).

Lists 'not a fit if' cases: teams needing production A2A execution/auth/secure transport, teams wanting validated performance on real heterogeneous endpoints, or teams needing a complete A2A client with discovery, streaming and cancellation.
Restates the operational boundary: the adapter does not send tasks, authenticate endpoints, verify signatures, stream, poll, cancel or transfer artifacts.
Shows an old star figure (4.3k) and 'last updated 1mo ago', so treat both as snapshots.

competitors.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification, latest released version 1.0.0
key_points: The protocol is layered: Layer 1 canonical data model as Protocol Buffer messages (spec/a2a.proto is the single authoritative normative definition), Layer 2 abstract operations, Layer 3 protocol bindings for JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON/REST.
Discovery is a well-known URI: the Agent Card is served at https://{server_domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json (a permanent URI), plus registries/catalogs and direct configuration.
JSON-RPC binding is JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S) with PascalCase methods and Server-Sent Events for streaming; REST binding uses application/a2a+json and URLs such as POST /message:send.
The A2A-Version service parameter is transmitted as an HTTP header (example shows A2A-Version: 0.3), which is what version negotiation and extension handling key off.
Current released version is 1.0.0, with 0.3.0, 0.2.6 and 0.1.0 listed as previous versions.

stats.fact: Google launched the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol on 9 April 2025 with support and contributions from more than 50 technology partners, including Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, LangChain, MongoDB, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, UKG and Workday.

On 23 June 2025 the Linux Foundation announced the formation of the Agent2Agent project, seeded by Google's transfer of the A2A specification, SDKs and developer tooling, with Amazon Web Services, Cisco, Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow as founding members; more than 100 companies supported the protocol at that point.
A2A v1.0.0 shipped on 12 March 2026 as the first stable production-ready release; v1.0.1 followed on 28 May 2026.

A2A was accepted as a Growth Stage project at the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), operating under Linux Foundation-directed governance alongside sibling projects MCP, goose and AGENTS.md; the protocol is backed by over 150 organizations and runs in production across supply chains, financial services and mobile platforms.
The reference a2aproject/A2A repository had 25,976 stars, 2,639 forks, 265 open issues and last push 2026-10-01 (created 2025-03-25, Apache-2.0).

Sprix SAGE Router (github.com/wang2122/sprix-sage-router) was created 18 August 2026, published v0.1.0 the same day and v0.3.0 on 28 August 2026, and stood at 4,261 stars, 186 forks, 181 watchers, 8 contributors, 43 commits, 2 open issues, MIT licence, last push 2026-08-28. Python 3.10+ and zero runtime dependencies.

Third-party star figures for SAGE conflict because they are dated snapshots from a fast-moving repo: about 677 stars on 2026-08-22 (heatdrop body text), 3,456 stars / 401 forks on 2026-09-05 (moclaw), 3,814 on 2026-09-07 (reveneau), and 4,261 from the GitHub API on 2026-10-01. Always cite a figure with its date.
stats.source: Cross-check of heatdrop, moclaw and GitHub REST API on 2026-10-01

stats.fact: In the project's 1,000-checkpoint, five-seed trajectory replay, progress-aware SAGE scored utility 0.298 +/- 0.021 with 0.059 wasted work, a 58.4% switch rate and a 23.3% deadline-miss rate; the progress-masked variant scored 0.291 +/- 0.021 with 0.104 wasted work, an 80.1% switch rate and 23.6% deadline miss.

Naive baselines in the same replay: always-continue reaches only 0.085 utility with a 34.4% deadline-miss rate; always-handoff reaches 0.290 utility but wastes 0.130 of the work, the worst in the table; the hidden-state dynamic oracle reaches 0.375 utility with a 19.6% deadline-miss rate.

In the controlled intervention that holds task, agents, difficulty, artifact portability, budget and deadline fixed while changing only in-flight completion from 0.0 to 0.9, progress-aware minus progress-masked utility grows from +0.0000 to +0.0684, and the two policies are identical when completion is zero.

Tracking trust per agent per requirement beats one reputation score per agent after 500 observations per seed in the heterogeneous specialist setting: Brier 0.0125 +/- 0.0018 and selection regret 0.0094 +/- 0.0008 versus 0.0355 +/- 0.0008 and 0.0310 +/- 0.0359. In the homogeneous negative control both methods show zero routing regret, so the benchmark does not manufacture an advantage when specialisation is absent.

On the 2,500 independent-task regression suite, learned SAGE reaches quality 0.613 +/- 0.005 versus 0.577 for a greedy team, 0.491 for static SAGE, 0.445 for advertised-skill solo and 0.332 for incumbent-only; learned SAGE with a random prior drops to 0.447, which exposes prior sensitivity.

The project states its own numbers are regression and falsification evidence only: both evaluators are authored with the project and are not evidence of real-world superiority. A publishable evaluation still requires repeated checkpointed executions on heterogeneous real endpoints and an independently governed artifact judge.

The prototype deliberately does not transmit tasks, authenticate endpoints or verify signatures; an A2A client remains responsible for message/send, streaming, polling, cancellation, idempotency, secret isolation, human approval and artifact evaluation. 'Do not treat a successful routing decision as a successful task execution.'

On one Apple Silicon development machine, the default top-12 configuration routed the six-requirement case in a median 78.4 ms at 20 agents, 78.9 ms at 40 and 80.1 ms at 80 (three repeats; environment-specific, not a latency SLA, and excluding candidate retrieval, network calls and executor latency).

Independent state-aware routing research (STRMAC) reports up to 23.8% improvement over baselines and up to 90.1% less data-collection overhead than exhaustive search, by encoding interaction history and agent knowledge separately and selecting one agent per step.

Dynamic coalition formation and communication pricing for skill-based agent systems models selection as a cooperative game U(C|x)=V(C|x)-sum(c_i); greedy routing reaches 99.5% of brute-force-optimal utility while activating 1.96 of 8 agents on average, versus 38.8% for full broadcast, and performance falls to 66% under strong submodularity violations or noisy value estimates.

Modality-native routing in A2A networks (MMA2A) lifts task completion to 52% versus 32% for a text-bottleneck baseline on the 50-task CrossModal-CS benchmark at a 1.8x latency cost, but an ablation replacing LLM reasoning with keyword matching erases the gap entirely (36% vs 36%).

The A2A Agent Card is discovered at https://{domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json (renamed from agent.json in v0.3, RFC 8615), transport is JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S) with Server-Sent Events for streaming plus webhook push notifications, and a task moves from submitted to working to a terminal state - the caller must emit a terminal event or the client waits forever.

Running the project's own replay locally (1,000 trajectories, 5 seeds x 200, evaluator checkpoint_artifact_v1) reproduced the README table exactly: progress-aware SAGE utility 0.298 +/- 0.021 with added cost 0.191, recovery latency 0.425, wasted work 0.059, switch rate 58.4% and deadline miss 23.3%; progress-masked 0.291 +/- 0.021 with added cost 0.204, recovery latency 0.434, wasted work 0.104, switch rate 80.1% and deadline miss 23.6%.
stats.source: Local execution of github.com/wang2122/sprix-sage-router at commit bdc9c24, 2026-10-01 (benchmark_dynamic.py --json)

stats.fact: The mode mix behind those headline numbers is the clearest single insight in the study: checkpoint-aware routing chose SELF in 416 of 1,000 trajectories (42%) versus 199 (20%) for the progress-masked variant, and HANDOFF in 442 (44%) versus 665 (66%), while COLLABORATE stayed almost identical at 142 (14%) versus 136 (14%). Checkpoint awareness mainly teaches the router to leave a task where it is, not to collaborate more.
stats.source: Local execution of benchmark_dynamic.py JSON output (trajectory_replay.mode_mix), 2026-10-01 - not published in the project README

stats.fact: The dynamic oracle in the same replay chose SELF only 100 times (10%), COLLABORATE 379 (38%) and HANDOFF 521 (52%) - so the oracle is the most handoff-happy policy in the comparison, which is a useful counterweight to the intuition that better information always means keeping the incumbent.
stats.source: Local execution of benchmark_dynamic.py JSON output (trajectory_replay.mode_mix), 2026-10-01

stats.fact: Local execution on a container CPU measured median route latency of 23.27 ms at 5 agents and 244.23 / 252.94 / 252.77 ms at 20 / 40 / 80 agents with candidate_limit=12 - roughly 3x the README's Apple Silicon figures, but flat from 20 to 80 agents, which reproduces the bounded-prefilter claim rather than the absolute latency.
stats.source: Local execution of benchmark_scaling.py at commit bdc9c24, 2026-10-01

angles: Lead with the mode mix, not the utility column: checkpoint awareness changed the route choice far more than the score - SELF rose from 20% to 42% of decisions and HANDOFF fell from 66% to 44%, while the utility gap stayed inside the error bars. That is the mechanism behind 'knowing what is done teaches the router to leave things alone', and no existing article has it.
The runtime gap: A2A standardised discovery (a directory problem) but never said who does the work after the handshake - SAGE is the policy layer above the protocol, not a competitor to it.

Run it yourself, not just read it: the repo has no runtime dependencies, so a reader can clone it, run demo.py and see COLLABORATE selected with a real utility number in one command - no article in the current top results actually walks through execution output.

Checkpoint-aware rerouting is the honest claim and the honest number: utility barely moves between progress-aware and progress-masked (0.298 vs 0.291), but wasted work drops about 43% and the switch rate falls from 80.1% to 58.4%. Knowing what is already done mostly teaches the router to leave things alone - that reframing is the insight, not the leaderboard.

Why the router must have a reason NOT to recruit: every added participant adds messages, dependencies, conflicting estimates and an attribution problem when the result fails; SAGE prices coordination overhead and context-transfer loss explicitly.

Requirement-conditioned trust as the anti-pattern fix: one reputation score per agent does not transfer across skills, and the repo has a homogeneous negative control proving the benchmark does not invent an advantage where specialisation is absent.

The attribution gap nobody has closed: outcome feedback cannot currently separate agent quality from task difficulty from the router's own prior choices. Without logged propensities and off-policy evaluation, learning can be self-confirming.

Date every number: star counts for this repo swung from about 677 (22 Aug) to 4,261 (1 Oct) 2026, and two of three competitor articles quote pre-release benchmark tables that no longer match v0.3 - a practical lesson in citing snapshots.

The permission-first rule that most routing demos get wrong: hard filters on permissions, availability and failure state run BEFORE any capability scoring, and a high learned score can never override them.

Decision, not execution: a routing decision is not a task execution. A production A2A client must still own authentication, streaming, polling, cancellation, idempotency, secret isolation, human approval and artifact evaluation.

Where a state-aware router is the wrong tool: short deterministic workflows, single-agent tasks, no calibrated outcome evaluator, or any setting where you cannot observe artifact quality - the router's checkpoint signal does not exist without an evaluator.

faq.a: It is the runtime decision of which agent or agent team should execute a task in an Agent2Agent network - covering who owns the task, who joins, and what topology connects them. A2A itself standardises discovery and transport; a router supplies the missing policy layer.

faq.q: Does the A2A protocol include a router?
faq.a: No. A2A v1.0 defines Agent Cards, messages, tasks, artifacts, authentication and transport bindings. It tells you which agents exist and how to reach them; it does not decide who should do the work after execution has started.

faq.q: What is the difference between SELF, COLLABORATE and HANDOFF?
faq.a: SELF keeps the task with the incumbent. COLLABORATE keeps the incumbent as owner and recruits peers to cover missing requirements. HANDOFF gives a peer full ownership. They share one utility function, so the choice is a comparison, not a hard-coded state machine.

faq.q: How do you decide when to hand off an in-flight agent task?
faq.a: Estimate how much of the current owner's work a new owner can actually reuse: completed fraction times artifact portability, plus observed partial quality. Then compare the specialist advantage against the redo cost, transfer loss, coordination overhead and any deadline or budget impact.

No. It describes itself as an early-stage research preview. It returns a routing decision and a transport-neutral plan but does not send tasks, authenticate endpoints, verify signatures, stream, poll or cancel. Production use needs an A2A client, calibrated evaluators, identity and signing, observability and human approval gates.

research_notes: Brief assembled 2026-10-01 from live HTTP retrieval plus local execution of the cloned repository; no browser rendering and no browser installs were used. Primary evidence is the repository itself (README, ALGORITHM.md, docs/, source) plus GitHub REST API provenance counts, so every SAGE number in this brief is either project-published or reproduced locally and is labelled accordingly. The three competitor articles (heatdrop, dev.to, moclaw) are independent but all landed within four days of the repo's 18 August 2026 launch, so each carries early star figures and pre-v0.3 benchmark tables - always date a number and prefer the API figure. Star counts swing wildly on this repo (about 677 on 2026-08-22 to 4,261 on 2026-10-01), which is itself a useful point for the article. SAGE's own benchmark environments are project-authored; the ALGORITHM.md evidence boundary says so explicitly, and the article should repeat that rather than paraphrase it as a weakness. The write-side differentiators are (1) an executable walkthrough from Agent Card to ExecutionPlan with real printed output, (2) an honest benchmark reading that separates design rigor from synthetic numbers by leading with wasted work and switch rate rather than the overlapping utility scores, (3) the attribution gap that neither the repo nor its reviewers have closed, and (4) a clear permission-first rule plus a 'wrong tool' section that the existing coverage omits. The full benchmark_dynamic replay was completed locally and reproduced every README figure to three decimals, which lets the article say 'reproduced' rather than 'quoted' - but the study is still synthetic and the repo's own scope string says so, so keep the framing honest. The mode-mix numbers (SELF 42% vs 20%, HANDOFF 44% vs 66%, COLLABORATE flat at 14%) are the strongest original material in this brief because they are absent from the README and from all four competitor pieces.
